A fourth type of cancer that arises in the pancreas is the intraductal tubulopapillary neoplasm. This type was recognised by the WHO in 2010 and constitutes about 1–3% of all pancreatic neoplasms. Mean age at diagnosis is 61 years (range 35–78 years). About 50% of these lesions become invasive. Diagnosis depends on histology, as these lesions are very difficult to differentiate from other lesions on either clinical or radiological grounds.[50]

### Palliative care

[edit]

Palliative care is medical care which focuses on treatment of symptoms from serious illness, such as cancer, and improving quality of life.[106] Because pancreatic adenocarcinoma is usually diagnosed after it has progressed to an advanced stage, palliative care as a treatment of symptoms is often the only treatment possible.[107]


Palliative care focuses not on treating the underlying cancer, but on treating symptoms such as pain or nausea, and can assist in decision-making, including when or if hospice care will be beneficial.[108] Pain can be managed with medications such as opioids or through procedural intervention, by a nerve block on the celiac plexus (CPB). This alters or, depending on the technique used, destroys the nerves that transmit pain from the abdomen. CPB is a safe and effective way to reduce the pain, which generally reduces the need to use opioid painkillers, which have significant negative side effects.[3][109]

The most common complication of surgery is difficulty in emptying the stomach.[3] Certain more limited surgical procedures may also be used to ease symptoms (see Palliative care): for instance, if the cancer is invading or compressing the duodenum or colon. In such cases, bypass surgery might overcome the obstruction and improve quality of life but is not intended as a cure.[12]

#### PanNETs

[edit]

The 2010 WHO classification of tumors of the digestive system grades all the pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (PanNETs) into three categories, based on their degree of cellular differentiation (from "NET G1" through to the poorly differentiated "NET G3").[22] The U.S. National Comprehensive Cancer Network recommends use of the same AJCC-UICC staging system as pancreatic adenocarcinoma.[64]: 52 Using this scheme, the stage-by-stage outcomes for PanNETs are dissimilar to those of the exocrine cancers.[65] A different TNM system for PanNETs has been proposed by the European Neuroendocrine Tumor Society.[22]



## Prevention and screening

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

For locally advanced and metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinomas, which together represent over 80% of cases, numerous trials comparing chemotherapy regimes have shown increased survival times, but not to more than one year.[2][86] Overall five-year survival for pancreatic cancer in the US has improved from 2% in cases diagnosed in 1975–1977, and 4% in 1987–1989 diagnoses, to 6% in 2003–2009.[110] In the less than 20% of cases of pancreatic adenocarcinoma with a diagnosis of a localized and small cancerous growth (less than 2 cm in Stage T1), about 20% of Americans survive to five years.[19]


About 1500 genes are linked to outcomes in pancreatic adenocarcinoma. These include both unfavorable genes, where high expression is related to poor outcome, for example C-Met and MUC-1, and favorable genes where high expression is associated with better survival, for example the transcription factor PELP1.[51][52]

Exceptions to this are the functioning PanNETs, where over-production of various active hormones can give rise to symptoms (which depend on the type of hormone).[31]

* Obesity – a body mass index greater than 35 increases relative risk by about half.[12][40]

Pancreatic adenocarcinoma and the other less common exocrine cancers have a very poor prognosis, as they are normally diagnosed at a late stage when the cancer is already locally advanced or has spread to other parts of the body.[2] Outcomes are much better for PanNETs: Many are benign and completely without clinical symptoms, and even those cases not treatable with surgery have an average five-year survival rate of 16%,[62] although the outlook varies considerably according to the type.[31]

The genetic events found in ductal adenocarcinoma have been well characterized, and complete exome sequencing has been done for the common types of tumor. Four genes have each been found to be mutated in the majority of adenocarcinomas: *KRAS* (in 95% of cases), *CDKN2A* (also in 95%), *TP53* (75%), and *SMAD4* (55%). The last of these is especially associated with a poor prognosis.[3] *SWI/SNF* mutations/deletions occur in about 10–15% of the adenocarcinomas.[2] The genetic alterations in several other types of pancreatic cancer and precancerous lesions have also been researched.[3] Transcriptomics analyses and mRNA sequencing for the common forms of pancreatic cancer have found that 75% of human genes are expressed in the tumors, with some 200 genes more specifically expressed in pancreatic cancer as compared to other tumor types.[51][52]

Pancreatic cancer has been associated with these other rare hereditary syndromes: Peutz–Jeghers syndrome due to mutations in the *STK11* tumor suppressor gene (very rare, but a very strong risk factor); dysplastic nevus syndrome (or familial atypical multiple mole and melanoma syndrome, FAMMM-PC) due to mutations in the *CDKN2A* tumor suppressor gene; autosomal recessive ataxia-telangiectasia and autosomal dominantly inherited mutations in the *BRCA2* and *PALB2* genes; hereditary non-polyposis colon cancer (Lynch syndrome); and familial adenomatous polyposis. * Chronic pancreatitis appears to almost triple risk, and as with diabetes, new-onset pancreatitis may be a symptom of a tumor.[3] The risk of pancreatic cancer in individuals with familial pancreatitis is particularly high.[3][42]

<fragment>

**Pancreatic cancer** arises when cells in the pancreas, a glandular organ behind the stomach, begin to multiply out of control and form a mass. These cancerous cells have the ability to invade other parts of the body.[9] A number of types of pancreatic cancer are known.[10]


The most common, **pancreatic adenocarcinoma**, accounts for about 90% of cases,[11] and the term "pancreatic cancer" is sometimes used to refer only to that type.[10] These adenocarcinomas start within the part of the pancreas that makes digestive enzymes.[10] Several other types of cancer, which collectively represent the majority of the non-adenocarcinomas, can also arise from these cells.[10]


About 1–2% of cases of pancreatic cancer are neuroendocrine tumors, which arise from the hormone-producing cells of the pancreas.[10] These are generally less aggressive than pancreatic adenocarcinoma.[10]

### Staging

[edit]

#### Exocrine cancers

[edit]

Pancreatic cancer is usually staged following a CT scan.[32] The most widely used cancer staging system for pancreatic cancer is the one formulated by the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) together with the Union for International Cancer Control (UICC). The AJCC-UICC staging system designates four main overall stages, ranging from early to advanced disease, based on TNM classification of **T**umor size, spread to lymph **N**odes, and **M**etastasis.[61]

Based on the comprehensive research I've conducted, I can provide you with information about the top cancers affecting women globally and their symptoms. However, I should note that while I found extensive cancer data, the most recent 2022-2024 global female-specific mortality rankings weren't available in the sources I accessed.

## **Top 5 Cancers by Mortality Rates in Women Worldwide**

Based on the available global cancer data and mortality patterns, here are the leading cancer deaths in women:

### **1. Lung Cancer**
**Global Impact:** Most deadly cancer worldwide with 1.8 million deaths globally in 2020, representing 18% of all cancer deaths. Women's survival rates are improving (22% five-year survival vs 16% in men).

### **2. Breast Cancer** 
**Global Impact:** 685,000 deaths globally in 2020. The most common cancer in women worldwide and a leading cause of female cancer deaths, particularly significant in developing countries.

### **3. Colorectal Cancer**
**Global Impact:** 551,000 deaths globally in 2018. Fourth most common cause of cancer death worldwide with significant impact on women.

### **4. Stomach Cancer**
**Global Impact:** 783,000 deaths globally in 2018 (both sexes). Third leading cause of cancer death globally, with women having better outcomes than men in some regions.

### **5. Pancreatic Cancer**
**Global Impact:** 411,600 deaths globally in 2015. Among the most deadly cancers with extremely low survival rates (12% five-year survival overall).

## **Symptoms Women Should Recognize**

### **1. Lung Cancer Symptoms**

**Early Warning Signs:**
- New persistent cough or change in existing cough pattern
- Shortness of breath, especially with activity
- Chest pain that's often dull and persistent in the same location
- Unexplained fatigue or weakness
- Hoarseness or voice changes

**Advanced Symptoms:**
- Coughing up blood (even small streaks in sputum)
- Recurrent respiratory infections
- Unexplained weight loss and loss of appetite
- Bone pain (if spread to bones)
- Headaches or seizures (if spread to brain)
- Superior vena cava syndrome (swelling of face, neck, upper body)

**Red Flag for Women:** Don't dismiss persistent cough as "just smoker's cough" or a lingering cold, especially if you have any smoking history.

---

### **2. Breast Cancer Symptoms**

**Early Warning Signs:**
- New lump or mass in breast or underarm area
- Change in breast size, shape, or contour
- Dimpling or puckering of breast skin
- Newly inverted nipple
- Red, scaly, or thickened skin on breast or nipple
- Clear or bloody nipple discharge

**Advanced Symptoms:**
- Breast pain or tenderness
- Swelling in the breast or armpit
- Skin changes resembling orange peel (peau d'orange)
- Changes in breast temperature (warmth)
- General symptoms like fatigue, weight loss

**Special Warning - Inflammatory Breast Cancer:** Sudden breast swelling, redness, and warmth (often mistaken for infection) requires immediate medical attention.

---

### **3. Colorectal Cancer Symptoms**

**Early Warning Signs:**
- Change in bowel habits lasting more than a few days
- Blood in stool (bright red or dark)
- Narrower than usual stools
- Persistent feeling of incomplete bowel evacuation
- Unexplained abdominal discomfort or cramping

**Advanced Symptoms:**
- Significant unexplained weight loss
- Fatigue and weakness (often due to anemia)
- Dark tarry stools or visible blood
- Persistent nausea or vomiting
- Feeling of fullness even after small meals
- Abdominal bloating and gas

**Red Flag for Women:** Any rectal bleeding or persistent change in bowel habits needs evaluation, regardless of age.

---

### **4. Stomach Cancer Symptoms**

**Early Warning Signs:**
- Persistent indigestion or heartburn
- Upper abdominal pain or discomfort
- Loss of appetite, especially for meat
- Nausea after eating
- Feeling full quickly after small meals

**Advanced Symptoms:**
- Unexplained weight loss (often significant)
- Yellowing of skin and eyes (jaundice)
- Vomiting blood or coffee-ground material
- Dark, tarry stools
- Difficulty swallowing
- Abdominal swelling or mass

**Red Flag for Women:** Persistent indigestion that doesn't respond to usual treatments, combined with weight loss, needs urgent evaluation.

---

### **5. Pancreatic Cancer Symptoms**

**Early Warning Signs (Often Subtle):**
- Unexplained weight loss
- Upper abdominal pain that may radiate to back
- New-onset diabetes, especially after age 50
- Loss of appetite
- Digestive problems

**Advanced Symptoms:**
- Yellowing of skin and eyes (jaundice)
- Itchy skin
- Light-colored stools and dark urine
- Severe abdominal or back pain that worsens when lying down
- Nausea and vomiting
- Blood clots (unusual swelling or pain in legs)

**Critical Red Flag:** New diabetes diagnosis after age 50, combined with weight loss or abdominal pain, should prompt immediate pancreatic evaluation.

---

## **When to Seek Medical Attention**

**Immediate Attention Needed For:**
- Any lump or mass in breasts/chest area
- Unexplained vaginal bleeding (between periods, after sex, after menopause)
- Coughing up blood
- Unexplained weight loss of 10+ pounds
- Persistent jaundice (yellow skin/eyes)
- New neurological symptoms (headaches, seizures, confusion)

**Within Days to Weeks For:**
- New persistent cough lasting more than 2-3 weeks
- Change in bowel habits lasting more than a few days
- Blood in stool
- Persistent indigestion or abdominal pain
- Difficulty swallowing

## **Prevention and Screening Recommendations**

- **Breast Cancer:** Monthly self-exams, annual clinical exams, mammograms starting at age 40-45
- **Colorectal Cancer:** Screening starting at age 45 (earlier with family history)
- **Cervical Cancer:** Pap tests every 3 years, HPV testing every 5 years
- **Lung Cancer:** Low-dose CT scans for high-risk smokers
- **General:** Maintain healthy weight, regular exercise, limited alcohol, no smoking

**Important Note:** Many cancers in women present with subtle symptoms that can be mistaken for less serious conditions. Trust your instincts - if something feels "off" or "different," seek medical evaluation promptly. Early detection significantly improves outcomes for all these cancer types.
